newsitem.title: CROATIA: Banks in Croatia face tough competition, mergers.
newsitem.headline: Banks in Croatia face tough competition, mergers.

text.p: Croatia's banking system will in near future face intensified competition that will force some of the numerous small banks to merge or specialise to survive, bankers and analysts said on Wedsnesday.

"It is clear there are more banks now (in Croatia) than there need to be, and a lot of them don't quite know what they want to do," said Evan Kraft, U.S. banking expert and consultant to the National Bank of Crotia (NBH).

"In the next few years, there is going to be intensified competition... There are so many banks here and more are clearly going to come, especially foreigners," he told Reuters on the fringes of a three-day Croatian Financial Forum.

Six Western banks, including Austrian Investment Bank, Raiffeisen Bank Austria and French Societe Generale, have opened branches in Croatia since 1995, when Zagreb troops crushed a four-year old rebellion of its Serb minority.

Furthermore, four of the largest commercial banks have been or are currently being overhauled and Zagrebacka Banka, enlisted with SEAQ international in London in 1996. Its 1/10 Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) there fetched $25.525 on Wednesday.

"Right now, small banks, unable for a considerable expansion, are living off large spreads between active and passive interest rates," Velimir Sonje, head of NBH's research and statistics department, told the Forum.
Average lending rates in Croatia, on the rise in 1994 and 1995, went down from above 20 percent to below 10 percent last year.
"The movements of lending rates will determine the future of the banking system in Croatia," Sonje said.

"Small banks are either going to have to find their particular market niche or join up with a bigger bank," said Kraft, quoting venture capital and Western-style dealing with rich individuals as some of the possibilities for small banks.

"On the whole the prospect is not so gloomy... The good thing about it is that if a small bank fails it doesn't have too big an effect on the system," Kraft said. -- Zoran Radosavljevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
